references.title: Dora: Sampling and benchmarking for 3d shape variational auto-encoders
references.why: Establishes the baseline for evaluating 3D shape VAEs, highlighting the prior difficulty in balancing reconstruction quality with computational efficiency in latent spaces.

references.title: Structured 3d latents for scalable and versatile 3d generation
references.why: Introduces the foundational concept of structured latents for 3D generation, which this paper extends with the more compact O-Voxel representation.

references.title: Xcube: Large-scale 3d generative modeling using sparse voxel hierarchies
references.why: Demonstrates the prior use of sparse voxel hierarchies for large-scale 3D modeling, providing the architectural context for the sparse compression techniques used in this work.

history.visible_observation: The slide displays the title 'The Rigid Box Problem' and presents 'Figure 1' from a research paper. The figure consists of three main sections: a 'Reconstruction' panel showing a complex mechanical object (resembling a turbine or engine part) with visible internal structures and open holes, a 'Generation' panel showing a robot figure with material overlays, and a graph panel on the right. The full caption for Figure 1 is visible at the bottom of the image, confirming that the 'Left' panel demonstrates the reconstruction of a 1536³ asset and explicitly mentions the preservation of 'enclosed structures (shown in the second row)'.

The frames display a slide titled 'History of 3D Compression' featuring two scatter plots comparing '1/Mesh Distance' and 'Normal PSNR' against 'Number of Tokens'. The x-axis is logarithmic, spanning 1K to 100K tokens. The legend in the second frame identifies the data series as 'Ours' (purple diamond), 'Trellis' (orange x), 'Dora' (blue circle), 'SparseFlex' (red plus), and 'Direct3D-S2' (green square). The caption below the plots explicitly compares 'XCube' and 'Dora-VAE', stating that XCube uses over 10,000 tokens while Dora-VAE uses 1,280 tokens.
issues: The caption claims to compare 'XCube', but 'XCube' does not appear in the legend; the legend lists 'Ours', 'Trellis', 'Dora', 'SparseFlex', and 'Direct3D-S2'.
The caption refers to 'Dora-VAE', but the legend labels the corresponding data point as 'Dora'.

The visual evidence does not support the caption's claim that XCube uses '>10,000 tokens'; the purple 'Ours' data points (which the caption likely misidentifies as XCube) are plotted in the 10K to 100K range, but the label 'XCube' is absent from the figure itself.

The visual evidence contradicts the 'dense purple dots' description; the purple markers are distinct diamonds, and the 'high-token' cluster in the top right is dominated by red markers (SparseFlex), not purple.

history.visible_observation: Frame 1 displays the full source figure (Figure 3) on a slide, showing the bidirectional conversion between 3D assets and O-Voxel, along with the 'Shape: Flexible Dual Grid' and 'Material' panels. Frame 2 zooms in specifically on the 'Shape: Flexible Dual Grid' panel, clearly showing the step-by-step process: constructing the primal grid, determining dual face existence, moving dual vertices, and connecting quads. The dual vertices are visible as dots inside the voxel cells, and the faces are shown as quads connecting them.

The frame displays a slide titled 'From Mesh to Latent: A Concrete Example' featuring a central composite image of a wisteria trellis. The composite is divided into three horizontal rows: the top row shows a small inset reference image and a large PBR render of the trellis; the middle row displays a colorful visualization (likely a normal map or latent representation); and the bottom row shows a multi-view strip of the trellis from different angles. To the right, a 'Zoom location' inset references 'Figure 5 - p.7'. Below the image, text identifies the asset as a 'Wisteria trellis asset with reference, normal map, PBR render and multi-view row'. Pixel-art avatars of Maya and Aiden are in the bottom corners.
issues: The 'visual' plan defines three specific nodes ('Reference', 'Normal Map', 'PBR Render'), but the rendered frame does not display these labels on the image itself; the viewer must rely on the caption text below the image to identify the different visualizations.

The 'Zoom location' inset in the top right corner references 'Figure 5 - p.7', which is likely a citation error (pointing to the wrong figure number) or a confusing reference for a general audience, as the main visual is the focus of the current explanation.

history.visible_observation: The frame displays a title 'Evidence: Speed and Quality' and a central panel containing two stacked scatter plots. The x-axis is labeled 'Number of Tokens' and the y-axes are '1 / Mesh Distance' (top) and 'Normal PSNR' (bottom). A legend identifies five methods: Ours, Trellis, Dora, SparseFlex, and Direct3D-S2. The 'Ours' method (purple diamonds) appears in the upper-left region of the plots, indicating high fidelity metrics with low token counts. The other methods are clustered in the lower-right or mid-right regions. A small inset on the right shows a thumbnail of the full source figure (labeled 'Figure 1') with a box highlighting the current plot area. A caption below the plots states that the method achieves high fidelity with fewer tokens.
issues: The beat claims the x-axis is 'lower is better/compact' and y-axis is 'higher is better', but the plot's y-axis is '1 / Mesh Distance'. While higher values indicate better performance (lower distance), the label itself is an inverse metric, which might confuse a viewer expecting a direct 'Fidelity' label without explanation.

The beat references specific data points like '9.6K tokens' and '1024^3 resolution'. While the 'Ours' points are near the 10K mark on the log-scale x-axis, the specific '9.6K' value and the '1024^3' resolution are not explicitly printed on the visible plot or caption in this frame; they are inferred from the source text rather than visible evidence.

The beat mentions 'Trellis or Dora' points requiring '2.0K to 225K' tokens. While Trellis (orange) and Dora (blue) are visible, the specific range '225K' is not clearly legible or distinct in the cluster at the far right of the x-axis (which ends around 100K-200K visually), making the specific upper bound hard to verify from the image alone.
